actions.name: Guided camera inspection of plantar lesion (close-up, good lighting)
actions.result: Left plantar heel/midfoot: single pigmented macule/patch ~11 mm, irregular asymmetric border, variegated brown-black to tan color. On close review of the submitted photos, pigment appears to track along the skin ridges rather than the furrows between them (parallel ridge pattern) - a pattern favoring melanoma over a benign acral nevus, though in-person dermoscopy is required for definitive distinction. No surface ulceration, bleeding, or satellite lesions visible on this image.

actions.name: ABCDE assessment from photographs
actions.result: Asymmetry present; Border irregular/notched; Color variegated (two shades brown-black); Diameter ~11 mm; Evolving per patient report (growth over ~12 months). Meets multiple ABCDE criteria.

actions.name: Request additional photos: close-up with ruler/coin for scale, oblique lighting, and dermatoscope-free macro shot
actions.result: Patient submits additional images; lesion measures approximately 11 x 9 mm using coin for scale; borders remain irregular; no change in color pattern noted between images taken 2 weeks apart.

actions.name: Guided camera survey of total body skin (arms, legs, trunk, scalp part lines) for other pigmented lesions
actions.result: No other atypical pigmented lesions identified on patient-performed survey; several scattered benign-appearing seborrheic-type and nevus lesions on trunk, none concerning by patient description and camera review; limited by lighting and patient's inability to visualize own back fully.

actions.name: Inspect regional area for satellite lesions or in-transit nodules on left foot/ankle (patient self-palpation)
actions.result: No palpable nodules, no satellite pigmentation, no ulceration reported or visualized on left foot or ankle.

actions.name: Guided self-palpation of inguinal and popliteal lymph node regions
actions.result: Patient reports no palpable lumps or tenderness in left groin or behind left knee.

actions.name: Camera inspection of neck lesions (razor bumps)
actions.result: Multiple small (1-3 mm) firm hyperpigmented papules along the anterior and lateral neck in the beard-adjacent shave area, some with visible curled hairs; no pustules, no active drainage, no scarring plaques. Consistent with pseudofolliculitis barbae.

actions.name: Review prior dermatology or primary care notes for this lesion
actions.result: No prior dermatology visit on file. Primary care note from 8 months ago documents 'callus, left foot' with no biopsy or photography performed.

actions.name: Review family history documentation
actions.result: No first- or second-degree relatives with melanoma or other skin cancer per patient-reported history on file.

actions.name: Review medication list
actions.result: No current prescription medications; occasional ibuprofen for muscle soreness.

actions.name: Home ruler/tape measurement of lesion size with photo documentation
actions.result: Lesion measures 11 mm in greatest diameter by patient's own ruler measurement, correlating with submitted image.

actions.name: Review most recent complete blood count (baseline, from annual physical)
actions.result: WBC 6.1 x10^9/L (ref 4.0-11.0), Hgb 14.8 g/dL (ref 13.5-17.5), Platelets 240 x10^9/L (ref 150-400) — all within normal limits.

actions.name: Camera inspection of all 20 nails (fingers and toes) for pigmented streaks
actions.result: No longitudinal melanonychia or periungual pigmentation (Hutchinson sign) seen on any digit, including left great toe.

actions.name: Overall teledermatology risk stratification and triage decision
actions.result: Lesion is high-risk for acral lentiginous melanoma based on history (growth over 1 year), morphology (ABCDE-positive, parallel ridge pattern on photo), and acral location in a patient with deeply pigmented skin. Cannot be excluded or confirmed without in-person dermoscopy and tissue biopsy. Urgent in-person referral indicated within 2 weeks; teledermatology alone is insufficient for definitive diagnosis.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient recalls his primary care doctor examined the spot and called it a callus, giving him cream, without raising concern.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Primary care note from 8 months ago documents the lesion as 'callus, left foot' per patient's own description, with no photograph, no measurement, and no referral - confirming the lesion was underassessed rather than properly ruled out.
mismatches.teachingPoint: A benign-sounding label in the chart does not equal an adequate evaluation; acral pigmented lesions require photographic documentation, measurement, and a low threshold for referral, especially in patients with deeply pigmented skin where melanoma is often diagnosed late and at acral sites.

objectives.text: Elicit a complete lesion history including onset, change over time, and prior reassurance that delayed care-seeking.
Apply ABCDE criteria and recognize acral lentiginous melanoma risk features (parallel ridge pattern, acral site, growth) using submitted photographs despite the limits of teledermatology.
Perform a camera-guided regional and total-body skin survey to screen for satellite lesions, additional atypical nevi, and nodal spread within the limits of a remote exam.
Identify a mismatch between patient-reported reassurance from primary care and the actual documentation, and use it to reinforce the need for urgent in-person biopsy.
Correctly triage a high-risk pigmented acral lesion to urgent in-person dermoscopy and biopsy within two weeks, recognizing this is outside the scope of definitive diagnosis by telehealth alone.
Separately address the patient's secondary concern (pseudofolliculitis barbae) with appropriate camera exam and conservative counseling, without letting it distract from the urgent primary issue.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Pigmented lesion on left plantar heel/midfoot highly suspicious for acral lentiginous melanoma - requires urgent in-person dermoscopy and biopsy; cannot be diagnosed or excluded via telehealth alone.
differential: Acral lentiginous melanoma (leading concern given growth, ABCDE features, parallel ridge pattern on exam, acral site, patient demographic)
Benign acral nevus (possible but less likely given documented growth and irregular morphology)
Subungual/plantar hematoma (less likely - no trauma history, lesion has persisted and grown over a year rather than resolving)
Verruca (plantar wart) with secondary pigmentation (raised by colleague, but lacks typical verrucous surface change and does not explain the pigment pattern)

Talon noir (black heel) - typically resolves over weeks as skin exfoliates, inconsistent with a year of persistence and growth; the classic bedside paring test to confirm blood vs. melanin is not possible by telehealth, another reason this lesion cannot be excluded remotely
keyFindings: 11 mm pigmented plantar lesion with irregular border and two-tone brown-black coloration
Documented growth from ~5mm to ~11mm over approximately 12 months
On dermatologist review of photographs, pigment pattern appears to follow skin ridges (parallel ridge pattern), a feature favoring melanoma
No satellite lesions, no palpable regional lymphadenopathy, no nail pigment changes on remote exam
Prior primary care documentation labeled the lesion 'callus' without photography, measurement, or referral - inadequate prior evaluation
No personal or family history of melanoma; patient reports no sunburn history, consistent with the fact that acral melanoma arises independent of UV exposure
plan: Urgent in-person dermatology referral within 2 weeks for dermoscopic examination and excisional or punch biopsy of the plantar lesion
Counsel patient explicitly that teledermatology cannot rule in or rule out melanoma for this lesion and that photographs, while helpful, are not a substitute for in-person tissue diagnosis
Advise patient to avoid attempting to pare, shave, or otherwise disturb the lesion before biopsy
Document and communicate the discrepancy between the benign 'callus' label in the primary care note and the current concerning features, reinforcing the need for definitive histology

Provide brief conservative guidance for pseudofolliculitis barbae (reduce shave frequency, consider single-blade or electric razor, shave with the grain, warm compress, avoid tight close shaving) and offer dermatology follow-up or topical options if it does not improve, without this detracting from the urgent primary issue
Arrange safety-net follow-up to confirm the patient was successfully scheduled for in-person biopsy and to review results once available
redFlags: Documented lesion growth over 12 months on an acral, non-sun-exposed site in a patient with deeply pigmented skin - classic high-risk pattern for delayed melanoma diagnosis
Parallel ridge pattern identified by dermatologist on photograph review
Prior clinical encounter mislabeling the lesion as benign without appropriate documentation or referral
educationPoints: Melanoma in patients with deeply pigmented skin disproportionately arises at acral and mucosal sites (palms, soles, nail units) rather than sun-exposed areas, and is frequently diagnosed at a more advanced stage due to delayed recognition by patients and clinicians.

The parallel ridge pattern on acral dermoscopy (pigment following the ridges rather than the furrows) is a feature associated with acral melanoma, as opposed to the parallel furrow or lattice patterns seen in benign acral nevi; definitive distinction still requires in-person dermoscopy and histology - this pattern should be actively assessed by the examiner on photo review rather than assumed from the images alone.

Teledermatology has real limits for pigmented acral lesions: photograph quality, lack of true dermoscopy, inability to palpate or biopsy remotely, and inability to perform bedside tests such as the paring test for talon noir mean any lesion with concerning growth or morphology warrants in-person referral rather than reassurance by video alone.

A benign label in a prior chart note (e.g., 'callus') does not substitute for proper documentation (photography, measurement) or an adequate risk assessment, and should not anchor the current evaluation.

Pseudofolliculitis barbae is a separate, common, benign condition best managed conservatively and should be addressed without diverting attention or urgency from a potentially life-threatening lesion.

profile.title: Enlarging Pigmented Plantar Lesion in a Patient with Skin of Colour: Recognizing Acral Melanoma by Telehealth
profile.summary: A 35-year-old Nigerian-born nurse presents by video with a growing, irregularly bordered, two-toned pigmented lesion on his left sole that a colleague and his primary care physician previously dismissed as a wart or callus. The case teaches recognition of acral lentiginous melanoma risk features in deeply pigmented skin, the limits of teledermatology for definitive diagnosis, and appropriate urgent in-person triage, while also addressing a benign secondary complaint (pseudofolliculitis barbae) within scope.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Dallas, Texas, using a laptop camera with photographs pre-submitted via patient portal
